chunks: Which layers for power planes. The question: Which layers should power planes be on?
A power plane is a whole layer of copper that carries a supply voltage, such as 3. 3 volts, across the board.
It goes on an inner layer, right next to a ground plane, with the thinnest insulation the stackup allows.
Packed that close, the two planes act like a large capacitor with very little inductance, which helps feed the chips' sudden current demands.
Think of a town's water supply. Pumping water from a distant reservoir takes time, and the pipes resist sudden demand.
A water tower right in town answers instantly when everyone turns on a tap. The plane pair is the tower, sitting right beside the chips.
The decoupling capacitors are buckets you carry in, and they do most of the work at lower frequencies.
The analogy breaks in one place: the planes store only a little charge, and what makes them useful is that they can deliver it very fast.
Which element dominates at which frequency.

At low frequency the regulator and bulk capacitors set the impedance; mid-band ceramic capacitors take over; above roughly 100 megahertz only the plane pair and the package and on-die capacitance are effective.
The curve is schematic, not a calculation; the anti-resonance peaks between regions are why you need a plan, not just many capacitors. Use the interactive version below.
Capacitance: how much charge two nearby conductors store per volt. Closer plates store more ("What capacitance is").
Inductance: how strongly a path resists a sudden change in current. Impedance: how much the supply's voltage moves per amp of sudden current, in ohms. Lower is better.
Power distribution network (PDN): the planes, vias and decoupling capacitors that deliver current ("Why many decoupling capacitors, not one big one").
Target impedance: the PDN impedance you must stay under so the supply does not sag too much.
A 3. 3 volts supply may sag 5%, which is 0. 165 volts, when a chip suddenly draws 1 amps more. So the target is 0. 165 volts / 1 amps = 0. 165 ohms.
A 100 mm by 100 mm plane pair with 0. 1 mm of insulation has about 3. 8 nanofarads of capacitance. At 500 megahertz its impedance is about 0. 084 ohms, under the target.
With 1 mm of insulation it is 0. 38 nanofarads and 0. 84 ohms, five times over. That is the whole idea.
"Power planes go on inner layers, right next to a ground plane with a thin dielectric between them.
That pair forms a low-inductance capacitor that helps decoupling at high frequency and keeps current loops small.
In four layers that's layer 3 under the layer 2 ground; in six layers, layer 4 next to the layer 5 ground.
I keep full planes off the outer layers, use pours there for high-current rails, split inner planes for multiple rails and avoid routing fast signals across the splits."
